claims.text: Rapid synthesis establishes a kinetically trapped short-range chemical order in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Short-range chemical order mediates the local electronic structure.
The electronic structure associated with short-range order suppresses atomic diffusion at high temperature.
Kinetically trapped short-range order suppresses high-temperature phase segregation.
The laser-induced thermionic-emission reduction method produces uniformly mixed high-entropy nanoalloy particles approximately 1–3 nm in size on a carbonaceous support.
Atomic diffusion becomes activated at approximately 0.5–0.6 times the melting temperature.
Short-range chemical order reflects a uniform distribution of multiple metal species.
A specific valence-electron concentration stabilizes the electronic structure associated with the short-range order.
Rapid synthesis locks in a metastable, well-mixed atomic configuration with pronounced short-range order.
Short-range order tailors local bond environments and electronic density in a way that hinders atomic diffusion.
The short-range order reduces the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation.
After high-temperature annealing, rapidly synthesized nanoalloys will retain a single phase and a uniform elemental distribution.
Rapidly synthesized nanoalloys will exhibit less post-annealing phase segregation than slowly synthesized counterparts.
Slow reaction kinetics in conventional synthesis promote phase segregation or chemical inhomogeneity in nanoalloys.
The predicted stabilization is limited to nearly equimolar particles smaller than approximately 5 nm.
The stabilization may differ for larger particles, compositionally skewed particles, or conditions dominated by oxidation.
The relative contributions of electronic-structure effects and kinetic trapping are not quantitatively established and may depend on synthesis parameters.
Comparable segregation in rapid- and slow-synthesis samples, or failure of the rapid-synthesis sample to retain enhanced short-range order, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
